first.rationale: Two of the three current problems are funnel-internal (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so a single onboarding intervention plausibly moves both; memory_86 and memory_31 both point this direction, and memory_91 (activation messaging) would only address the downstream symptom. Promotional pricing (memory_73) is the salient reflex against the competitor's entry pricing, but discounting to price-sensitive SMBs is the option most likely to buy short-term acquisition at the cost of the primary objective (sustainable long-term QUALIFIED revenue), and it would anchor price in the segment most likely to churn; I am declining it rather than spending scarce verification on it. Referral incentives (memory_57) and enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) are sound but address neither of the two declining metrics this quarter. I spend the single verification pull on memory_86 because it is the record my chosen action rests on and it carries a specific, decision-relevant failure mode: 'improved completion rates' may be a funnel-metric artifact. Removing required fields and steps mechanically raises completion and can raise raw activation counts while degrading lead qualification, data capture used for routing, and eventual conversion to paid — i.e. the memory could be true as stated and still not support the objective. I want the original record to show whether the day-52 lift was tracked through to revenue/retention or stopped at completion and time-to-value, what segment and baseline it ran on, and whether any fields cut were qualification-bearing. Note also that all six memories are 15-64 days stale and were consolidated under pre-competitor market conditions; the current declines are evidence that at least some of those conditions have shifted, so I treat the inherited priors as directional rather than as settled effect sizes. Accordingly: standard experiment, not broad rollout, with success defined on qualified-revenue-relevant outcomes (activation to first meaningful action, trial-to-paid, 30-day retention) rather than completion rate alone, and a guardrail on lead-quality/routing metrics. If verification shows memory_86 measured only completion and time-to-value, I will narrow to a small guarded test that strips only non-qualification fields, and keep activation_messaging (memory_91) as the fallback since it lifts week-one engagement without touching the qualification gate.

final.rationale: Verification partially resolved my concern in favor of the action. exp_86 did not stop at the funnel metric: alongside completion +13% and time-to-value -2.1 days it reports 30-day retention +3%, which is the guard against the 'completion is an artifact of removing friction' failure mode I was worried about. Accounts that came through the shortened flow stuck around, so the lift was not purely mechanical. That raises my confidence enough to commit the slot to simplify_onboarding. What verification did NOT establish, and what I am therefore still treating as open: the record shows no trial-to-paid conversion, no revenue per account, and no lead-quality or routing metric. 30-day retention is a proxy for value but not for QUALIFIED revenue, which is the stated objective; it is possible to retain more low-value self-serve accounts while degrading the qualification data that routes larger accounts to sales (cf. memory_44, where the demo-request path outperformed self-serve on pipeline quality). So the specific risk I keep live is that cutting qualification-bearing fields improves the self-serve funnel while quietly starving the enterprise path. The experiment will therefore strip friction and non-essential steps but preserve fields used for qualification and routing, and will carry an explicit guardrail on demo-request rate and inbound lead quality. Also unresolved by the archive: exp_86 ran on day 52, before the competitor's entry pricing, and its baseline is a healthier funnel than today's (-4% completion, -6% activation). The effect size should be read as directional, not as a forecast; a +13% lift on a degraded baseline may recover less than it did before. This is why I am holding at standard experiment rather than broad rollout despite a 'confirmed' record — one confirmed prior run under different market conditions does not license skipping the measurement step. Onboarding remains the right single bet because it is upstream of both declining metrics and can move completion and activation together, where activation_messaging (memory_91) treats only the downstream symptom. I am still declining promotional_pricing (memory_73): matching a competitor's entry price on price-sensitive SMBs is the option that most directly trades long-term qualified revenue for short-term acquisition, and I did not spend verification on it because no plausible source record would change that judgment. Success criteria: activation to first meaningful action, trial-to-paid, and 30-day retention — not completion rate alone. If the lead-quality guardrail trips, halt and fall back to activation_messaging.
